# Assumption of Moses — Reader's Guide
**Guide:** HESED | **Category:** Pseudepigrapha (PS)

---

## At a Glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attribution** | Moses (speaking as a testamentary address to Joshua) |
| **Actual Composition** | c. 4 BCE – 30 CE (early 1st century CE; based on internal historical evidence) |
| **Language** | Latin (a single 6th-century manuscript); translated from Greek; possibly composed in Hebrew or Aramaic |
| **Audience** | Jewish communities under Roman rule, probably in Palestine |
| **Genre** | Testamentary literature; apocalyptic prophecy; farewell discourse |
| **Length** | 12 chapters (the surviving text is incomplete — beginning and end are lost) |
| **In One Sentence** | In his farewell address to Joshua, Moses reveals that all of Israel's history — from the conquest to the Roman era and beyond — was foreknown and scripted by God, who created the world for Israel's sake and will ultimately vindicate the righteous through cosmic theophany. |

---

## Sections Overview

### 1. Moses' Commission to Joshua (Chapter 1)
The text opens with Moses summoning Joshua and delivering to him the "books" he has written — a record of all that will happen to Israel from the conquest to the end of days. Moses identifies himself as the mediator of the covenant, appointed from before creation. The world was created on account of Israel; Moses was prepared from the foundation of the world to be the mediator of that covenant.

### 2. Prophetic History: Conquest to the First Exile (Chapter 2)
Moses prophesies Israel's entry into the land, the sin of the tribes, the building of the temple, and the Assyrian exile of the northern kingdom. The historical fulfillments are described in stylized, schematic terms rather than in the specific language of the prophets.

### 3. The Babylonian Exile (Chapter 3)
The destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile are described through a prayer of penitence that the eastern exiles will offer. Despite their sin, they will cry out to God and remember the covenant with the patriarchs.

### 4. Return and the Second Temple Period (Chapter 4)
The return from exile and the rebuilding of the temple are treated briefly. The second temple period is described without the glory of the first: the returning exiles offer impure sacrifices; the priesthood is compromised. The text does not idealize the restoration.

### 5. The Hasmonean Period and Its Corruption (Chapters 5–6)
Two overlapping figures of corruption appear: first, kings who are "not priests" but rule as if they are (the Hasmoneans); then a king described as "an insolent king who will not be of priestly stock" (widely identified as Herod the Great) whose reign brings unprecedented cruelty, execution of the elderly and young, and the slaughter of his own family. A second figure — probably representing the Roman general Varus, who crucified 2,000 rebels after Herod's death in 4 BCE — then punishes the Herodians.

### 6. A Time of Apostasy (Chapter 7)
The text describes a period of powerful but impious leaders ("men of pestilence and iniquity") who claim to be righteous while practicing deception, eating and drinking at the expense of others, and exploiting the poor. This section is often read as describing the Sadducean or priestly aristocracy of the early Roman period.

### 7. The Faithful and the Persecutors (Chapter 8)
A period of active persecution: rulers force Jews to abandon the Torah, forbid circumcision, crucify those who confess their Jewishness, compel them to carry idols. This section closely parallels the Antiochene persecutions of 167 BCE described in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees — but the placement in the text (after clearly Roman-era content) has generated intense debate. Some read it as a vaticinium ex eventu (prophecy after the fact) inserted out of sequence; others read it as a description of a future persecution expected under Rome.

### 8. Taxo and His Seven Sons (Chapter 9)
The most enigmatic passage in the text. A man named Taxo, from the tribe of Levi, addresses his seven sons: they have suffered enough, and rather than violate the Torah, they will go into a cave and die. Their death will trigger God's vengeance: "their blood will be avenged before the Lord." Taxo's name, his action, and his significance have generated more scholarly commentary than almost any other passage in this text. He is neither warrior nor messiah; his is a passive martyrdom — a deliberate refusal to comply, followed by death — and the claim is that this death will finally move God to act.

### 9. The Great Theophany (Chapter 10)
The climax of the book: when the end comes, God's kingdom will appear across all creation. The earth will shake, the sun will go dark, the moon will not give its light, the stars will be disturbed. God "the Eternal One" will rise from his throne and go forth from his holy dwelling with indignation and wrath. The mountains will be shaken to their foundations; the valleys will sink. The angel of intercession will arise and avenge Israel on its enemies. Israel will be raised up to the stars and look down on its enemies in Gehenna.

### 10. Joshua's Lament and Moses' Reply (Chapters 11–12)
Joshua, overwhelmed, tears his garments and weeps. He asks: who will intercede for Israel when Moses is gone? Moses replies with a meditation on God's greatness, Israel's role in the covenant, and the certainty that God will not abandon his people. The text breaks off — the ending is lost.

---

## The World Behind the Text

The *Assumption of Moses* was composed in the early decades of the first century CE, in the shadow of Herod's death (4 BCE) and the subsequent Roman reorganization of Judea. The crucifixion of 2,000 rebels by Varus in 4 BCE appears to be reflected in chapter 6. The "insolent king" of chapter 6 matches Herod in his 37-year reign, his non-priestly origins, and the execution of family members.

The text stands in the tradition of **Deuteronomistic theology**: Israel's history is a covenant story, obedience brings blessing, disobedience brings exile, and God will ultimately restore. But the *Assumption of Moses* pushes this framework into apocalyptic territory: restoration will not be achieved through human military action (as in the Maccabean model) but through God's direct cosmic intervention, triggered perhaps by the passive martyrdom of the righteous.

The text survives in a single, damaged 6th-century Latin manuscript discovered in Milan in 1861, which itself is a translation from Greek, probably composed from a Hebrew or Aramaic original. The beginning and end of the text are lost. What we have is a fragment — possibly about two-thirds — of the original work.

The reference in **Jude 9** to a dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over Moses' body is almost certainly from the conclusion of this text (or a closely related document sometimes called the *Testament of Moses*). Our surviving manuscript breaks off before that scene — a tantalizing loss.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The *Assumption of Moses* addresses a community experiencing political humiliation and religious pressure under Roman rule. Its message is threefold:

**1. History is not chaos.** Everything that has happened — the split of the kingdom, the Babylonian exile, the compromised priesthood, the brutality of Herod, the violence of Rome — was foreknown by God and told to Moses before it happened. The community's suffering is not a sign of divine abandonment; it is part of a scripted sequence.

**2. Human power is not the answer.** The text is strikingly anti-militaristic. The Maccabean revolt is treated without the heroism it receives in 1–2 Maccabees; the Hasmoneans are depicted as corrupt priest-kings. The climax of history comes not through armed resistance but through the passive faithfulness of Taxo — whose willingness to die rather than transgress the Torah finally provokes God's action.

**3. God will vindicate the righteous.** The theophany of chapter 10 is total and cosmic. The language is drawn from the great theophany texts of the Hebrew Bible (Psalms 18, 68; Micah 1; Habakkuk 3) and intensified. God himself rises from his throne. Israel is exalted to the stars. The enemies of Israel descend to Gehenna. This is not political realism — it is the language of hope in extremis.

---

## How to Read This Book

**Read it as a farewell discourse.** The genre is testament: a dying patriarch (here, Moses) speaks to his successor and reveals what lies ahead. This genre — found also in the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, in Jubilees, and in the Gospel of John's "farewell discourse" (John 13–17) — carries a specific authority claim: the dying speaker has privileged knowledge, and what he says will certainly come to pass.

**Track the historical referents in chapters 2–8.** The text is doing what apocalyptic literature typically does: presenting past events as future prophecy (*vaticinium ex eventu*) to establish credibility, and then extending that sequence into genuine prediction. The key question for each section is: when does the text shift from retelling known history to describing expected future events? Most scholars place that break around chapters 8–9.

**Sit with Taxo (chapter 9).** This is the most unusual figure in the text. He is not a warrior, not a king, not a prophet. He is a Levite who refuses to violate the Torah even to save his life and who expects his death to be the trigger for divine action. The theological logic — that passive martyrdom, not military heroism, will finally move God — is deeply countercultural in the ancient world and resonates with early Jewish martyrdom theology and with some strands of early Christian soteriology.

**Read chapter 10 aloud.** The theophany language is poetry in prose form. It is meant to overwhelm — to make the reader feel the magnitude of what is coming. Read it slowly. The movement from cosmic disruption (sun, moon, stars, mountains) to personal vindication (Israel raised to the stars) is the emotional and theological climax of the whole work.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

### With the Hebrew Bible / Old Testament
- **Deuteronomy 31–34** is the direct literary model: Moses' farewell, his appointment of Joshua, and the song and blessing that precede his death.
- The theophany language of **chapter 10** draws on Psalms 18, 68, and 97; Micah 1:3–4; Habakkuk 3; and Isaiah 34.
- **Daniel 7–12** provides the closest parallel in the canon for the schematic periodization of history and the expectation of cosmic divine intervention.
- The creation-for-Israel theology of **chapter 1** parallels **Exodus Rabbah** and other rabbinic texts that assert Israel's primacy in God's purposes.

### With the New Testament
- **Jude 9** refers to "the archangel Michael, when contending with the devil, disputed about the body of Moses" — a scene not in any surviving text but almost certainly drawn from the conclusion of the *Assumption of Moses* or a closely related work.
- The **passive martyrdom theology** of Taxo resonates with early Christian martyr theology and possibly with interpretations of Jesus' death as a death that triggers divine action.
- The **theophany of chapter 10** ("the Most High will arise... the earth will tremble") parallels the eschatological language of the Synoptic Gospels (Matt 24, Mark 13) and the book of Revelation.
- Moses as **pre-existent mediator** (ch. 1: "prepared from the foundation of the world") parallels early Christian language about Christ's pre-existence.

### With the Dead Sea Scrolls
- The **schematic periodization of history** and the identification of a corrupt priesthood both overlap with the Qumran community's self-understanding.
- The **solar calendar** and the **covenant mediator** theology resonate with Qumran texts, though no copy of the *Assumption of Moses* has been found at Qumran.

### With 1–2 Maccabees
- The *Assumption of Moses* and the Maccabean books cover overlapping history but with strikingly different theological conclusions: Maccabees valorizes armed revolt; the *Assumption* looks past it to passive martyrdom and divine action.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

1. **Moses as cosmic figure, not just lawgiver.** The claim in chapter 1 — that Moses was "prepared from the foundation of the world" to be the mediator of the covenant — is not in Deuteronomy. This is Second Temple Moses-theology, in which Moses' role is as large as creation itself. He is not merely the historical leader of the exodus; he is the cosmic pivot of God's plan for Israel.

2. **"The world was created for Israel's sake."** This is a real theological claim in chapter 1, not hyperbole. Several Second Temple Jewish texts make this assertion. It reflects a theology in which Israel is not merely one nation among others but the reason the cosmos exists. The apparent arrogance of this claim becomes more comprehensible when one remembers that the community making it is being crushed by Rome.

3. **Taxo is still unexplained.** The name "Taxo" has generated extensive scholarly debate. Proposed explanations include: a numerical cipher (Hebrew gematria), a transliteration of a Hebrew or Latin word, or a symbolic name. No consensus has been reached. This is one of the genuinely unresolved puzzles of ancient Jewish literature.

4. **The text does not describe a military messiah.** The *Assumption of Moses* is notable for what is absent: there is no king, no warrior, no "son of David" who defeats the enemies. God acts directly. This is one of the most "quietist" eschatologies in Second Temple Judaism — which makes it all the more striking that it was written during a period of active revolutionary ferment in Palestine.

5. **The Latin is already two translations removed from the original.** Every sentence should be read with the awareness that the original was almost certainly Hebrew or Aramaic, translated into Greek, and then into Latin. The cadences, wordplays, and literary effects of the original are largely inaccessible to us.

6. **We are missing the end.** The dispute over Moses' body (referenced in Jude 9) was presumably in the lost conclusion. The text we have breaks off mid-sentence in Moses' reply to Joshua. What we have is a magnificent fragment.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The *Assumption of Moses* was known to early Christians — Jude 9 virtually requires it — but it was never included in any biblical canon. Its exclusion follows the same pattern as most pseudepigrapha: it was recognized as pseudonymous (Moses did not write it), its theological claims (especially the creation-for-Israel theology) were not easily integrated into Christian theological frameworks, and it was simply lost — surviving in a single manuscript — after a period of early circulation.

The reference in Jude has led some scholars to suggest that the original, longer version (including the dispute over Moses' body) was authoritative enough for the NT writer to cite without introduction, the way Jude 14–15 cites 1 Enoch. But citation is not canonization; the book was used without being enshrined.

Its survival in one damaged manuscript is itself a story of narrow escape. Had the Milan manuscript not been found in 1861, this window into early first-century Jewish apocalyptic thought would have been closed entirely.

---

## Timeline

| Date (approx.) | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 4 BCE | Death of Herod the Great; Varus crucifies ~2,000 rebels — likely reflected in ch. 6 |
| c. 4 BCE – 30 CE | Probable composition of the *Assumption of Moses* |
| c. 50–70 CE | Letter of Jude written; quotes or alludes to the *Assumption* (Jude 9) |
| c. 2nd–3rd century CE | Origen, Clement of Alexandria, and others cite the text |
| c. 6th century CE | Latin manuscript copied (the sole surviving witness) |
| 1861 CE | Antonio Ceriani discovers and publishes the Milan manuscript |
| 1897 CE | R.H. Charles publishes the first major English critical edition |
| 1983 CE | John Priest's translation in *The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha* (Charlesworth, vol. 1) |
| 2000s CE | Continued scholarly debate on the date, provenance, and identity of Taxo |

---

*HESED notes: This guide was written for readers encountering the Assumption of Moses for the first time. The text's most lasting contribution may be its vision of passive martyrdom — the idea that faithfulness unto death, rather than armed resistance, is what finally moves God to act. This is a minority voice in Second Temple Judaism and a profoundly important one for understanding the theological world in which early Christianity emerged.*
